I'm thinking of checking the best rented B200 result (r6-s-ldef-nc-disp at 5.4/19.0/75.4) to study its approach, since fetching a kernel definition doesn't cost a GPU call, and sketching a grid design of 148*4 CTAs with 256 threads each.

I'm working out the memory layout: each half-warp pipelines rows with software prefetching, so loads for the next batch happen while reducing the current one, keeping register pressure manageable. I realize weight rows repeat every 48 tokens, so I can assign each half-warp a fixed head and make the weights stationary in registers, loaded just once. Then I'm mapping CTAs to (stream, head-group) combinations across Q/K and token groups, but running into the problem that 592 CTAs doesn't divide evenly into 6 combos, so I need to pick a persistent grid size like 588 that does.

I'm also checking that persistent CTA counts don't match well at the smallest sequence lengths — at 128 tokens the work per CTA is too fragmented to be worthwhile, so the one-shot launch approach is actually simpler there. But at medium sizes like 256 or 586 tokens, the number of 16-row tiles creates wave quantization tails (1.3 or 3+ waves), which is exactly the imbalance the persistent, prefetching design is meant to smooth out by distributing tiles evenly across resident CTAs.

Switching to row-level granularity instead of CTA-level: 9472 half-warps handling 24576 rows gives 2.6 rows each, still rounding to 3. But in a bandwidth-bound regime, if all loads for the extra row are issued upfront and overlapped, the imbalance might matter less than I initially thought since total bytes in flight dominate over per-thread latency.

I'm now comparing against CAKE's numbers - at 25 MB they hit 6.37 µs, and our r5 config is already matching that at 6.4-6.5 µs, so S-band gains from this optimization are looking uncertain. Checking the M-band throughput: 1024 tokens gets 6.1 TB/s, 2048 tokens gets 6.75 TB/s, and I'm now looking at the L-band numbers for 805 MB.

Since the evict_last stores mean the tail writes aren't fully counted, M-band seems like the best candidate for persistent-grid pipelining to help. I'm sketching a capped persistent kernel design: a grid sized to the GPU's CTA capacity, 256 threads per block with register limits tuned for occupancy, where each thread processes a batch of combined Q+K rows per iteration.

I'm working out prefetch batching—loading the next batch of rows while computing and storing the current one—and checking register pressure for different batch sizes. The tricky part is handling the weight stride across the Q-to-K boundary, since the head index needs to stay predictable so weights can be kept stationary in registers.

Since a thread switches between Q and K rows, I'd need both wq and wk available, so I'm considering a cheap select (FSEL) per element to choose the right weight rather than reloading from memory on each switch. With NHW as a multiple of 48 across G CTAs, this keeps the head index consistent enough for the stationary-weight approach to work.

Each pairing processes Q and K rows together, with the next pair's loads issued while the current pair computes, so roughly four rows' worth of data are in flight. I'm trying to work out register pressure: weights plus current and next row data push close to the 64-register limit under launch_bounds(256,4), so unrolling further to four rows plus prefetch would blow the budget. Seems like I need to back off on explicit prefetching to keep register usage manageable.

This mismatch means too many half-warps go idle, so I need to pick group size G more carefully—for 128 tokens, that works out to roughly 384 CTAs, each handling one item per half-warp with paired Q/K loads, matching the earlier 5.5 S configuration.

I'm also working out the weight-stationarity constraint requiring NHW divisible by 48 so G stays a multiple of 3, and figuring out how row indices map to head indices via modulo arithmetic on hw.

384 CTAs spread across 148 SMs isn't perfectly even either, so imbalance crops up regardless of the grid choice. Rather than keep reasoning about this abstractly, I should just add a tunable knob and actually benchmark a few configurations — the test machine is a rented B200, so I can get real timing data instead of guessing.

With k items per SM, the prefetch chain forms roughly a 2-deep pipeline since load i+1 gets issued right alongside load i, before item i's reduction stalls on its data — so the real latency is closer to ceil(k/2) DRAM round trips plus streaming overhead. I still need to figure out the size threshold for dispatching to the parent kernel versus using the capped kernel directly, which I'll determine empirically on the B200, and I want the capped kernel to handle all sizes so I can compare it against the alternative across the board.

Now I'm considering how to handle half-warps whose row count doesn't evenly divide, since diverging shuffle calls within a warp are unsafe with a full mask — I need all lanes to loop the same number of times and just predicate the loads and stores for the inactive ones.

Since the row counts work out evenly in this layout, both halves of a warp always stay in sync, so there's no actual divergence to worry about and the uniform-mask shuffle loop is safe to use as-is. Starting to sketch out the kernel template now.

Writing the persistent QK RMS norm kernel...

I need to check register pressure since the interleaved reductions for Q and K use quite a few live vectors simultaneously, hopefully staying under the register budget. On the host side, I'm working out the grid sizing formula so the group size stays a multiple of 48, balancing occupancy against the number of rows each thread needs to cover.

For the rounding logic, I want to confirm that rounding G up to a multiple of 3 never pushes it past the SM-derived cap, which checks out since k is chosen conservatively. I'll cache the SM count via a device query once rather than repeating it, and now I'm thinking about how to dispatch between the persistent kernel path and the parent-launch path based on token count, plus how to test multiple configs per shape band without an easy way to parameterize runs.

For an initial experiment I'll just run everything persistent with a fixed CTA-per-SM value and compare against the current best variant, then tune the threshold from there. I'm also checking whether the balanced-G computation actually balances well in practice -- working through a mid-size example, I'm seeing the CTA count doesn't divide evenly across SMs, leaving some SMs with one more CTA than others, which could hurt performance if the kernel is bandwidth-bound.

Thinking through whether a simpler rule, like capping G at some multiple of tokens, would keep occupancy full while bounding the per-thread workload imbalance to at most one item.

Trying a 192-thread CTA (6 warps) with 4 CTAs/SM divides evenly into 48*148, which works nicely. A 384-thread CTA also divides cleanly with 4 CTAs/SM, so either configuration satisfies the divisibility constraint.

Checking register budget though — with 1536 threads/SM, only about 42 registers per thread are available, which is too tight since I need roughly 60 registers per thread for the data values plus overhead.

So I'm leaning toward 256-thread CTAs with G=591, giving 4 CTAs per SM with one SM slightly imbalanced at 3 — a negligible tradeoff that lets me use 1024 threads/SM at 64 registers each, which fits the budget comfortably.

That confirms completion stays bandwidth bound for k≤2, with the pipeline going 2-deep for larger k — fine for the mid-range case with manageable peak memory footprint per SM. I'll skip checking other candidate kernels and just move straight to compiling, keeping the parent kernel unchanged for dispatch.

I'm setting up a caching helper to grab the SM count once via device attributes, then deriving the group cap and ensuring NHW divides cleanly by 48 given G is a multiple of 3. I still need to handle the edge case where the row count is smaller than 16*G by capping G appropriately, then move on to coding the persistent kernel version.

Writing persistent kernel loop...

Finishing the loop body and copying buffers for the next iteration, then I need to write the dispatch logic in the run function that picks between persistent and one-shot kernels based on token count, and confirm the entry point should be kernel.cu::run.

reasoning_details.text:
This variant runs slower everywhere, even at the smallest config where fewer CTAs with more per-thread work seems to hurt throughput compared to the parent version with more CTAs doing less each. I'm trying to figure out why — maybe it's related to occupancy or in-flight thread counts limiting parallelism.

By Little's law 128 KB/SM should be plenty, so maybe the real bottleneck is latency under load being much higher than expected, closer to 1.5-2 µs rather than nominal. The measured 6.2 TB/s suggests something else is throttling — maybe the scoreboard waits on the conditional loads inside the asm volatile blocks are structured in a way that stalls more than anticipated.

If the compiler doesn't rename registers across the loop-carried copy, the move instruction would wait on the pending load, collapsing the prefetch depth to effectively 1 item in flight instead of 2 — only 64 B/thread, 64 KB/SM, fully serialized on latency. That would explain the bandwidth gap, and matches what I'd expect from the generated LDG.256 sequence.

The real fix is to manually unroll by 2 using ping-pong buffers so there's no loop-carried copy at all: load item0, then alternate loading the next item and processing the current one, breaking cleanly when there's no more work, which guarantees the compiler can't insert a stalling move. I should keep this to two items in flight given the 64-register budget, and I still need to check why even the single-item case (small sizes) is slower than the parent kernel — roughly 4.5 vs 4.2 at 128 tokens with 384 CTAs of 256 threads.

Now I'm thinking the slowdown comes from poor SM occupancy balance: with 384 CTAs across 148 SMs that's an uneven 2-to-3 split causing real imbalance, whereas the parent's 768 CTAs divide more evenly into roughly 5-to-6 per SM, a smaller relative imbalance. So for S I should try smaller CTA sizes — maybe 128 or even 64 threads — to get finer-grained CTA counts that spread more evenly across SMs, like 1536 CTAs of 64 threads giving about 10.4 CTAs per SM, which should smooth out the imbalance considerably.

Given I only have a handful of GPU test runs left, I want to keep changes isolated — test the ping-pong fix across all sizes first to see its effect on M and L, rather than bundling in a thread-count change at the same time. I'll hold off on testing a 128-thread variant or tweaking G for now and stick to one variable at a time.

Deeper prefetch making things worse suggests it's not latency-bound per thread — more likely a DRAM locality or L2 partitioning issue with the persistent access pattern, and CAKE's findings back up that pipelined persistent doesn't help much at this scale. With only 5 GPU calls left, I'm leaning toward testing a capped-grid variant with minimal per-thread work to probe the S-band imbalance instead.

I'm also wondering if version 2's slowdown at small sizes comes from register pressure forcing spills to local memory rather than anything in the data path itself — that would explain the extra traffic. I'm now considering one more approach based on a different hypothesis: raise occupancy with a capped grid of CTAs per SM, assigning one row per item and treating Q and K rows as a combined range so the head index stays fixed within a block while the stream flips from Q to K partway through. This would keep both weight sets resident in registers alongside the current and next data rows, aiming to fit within the register budget needed for multiple CTAs to run concurrently per SM.

Loading weights from L1 per item instead of keeping them in registers would push the register count too high for good occupancy, landing around only 5 CTAs per SM. I'm starting to suspect the persistent kernel is losing to one-shot execution because finishing CTAs free up resources that let the scheduler keep memory traffic saturated, whereas the persistent approach's prefetching is constrained -- and the fact that more aggressive prefetching in v2 made things worse points to something like register spills rather than a scheduling issue.
